solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Blair book fan mail poor, member scoffs

indicators.note: to scoff is to gobble food down, so one piece swallows the other whole

parts.note: an arm is a limb, a member of the body

indicators.note: something poor is in a bad state, so these letters are knocked out of shape and rearranged

parts.note: the two words taken as written

explanation.surface: A disappointing postbag for a politician named Blair, sneered at by a party member.
explanation.walkthrough: Blair suggests Tony, but Eric Blair was George Orwell's real name. The limb opens after its first letter to take in the reworked letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Orwell, born Eric Arthur Blair, wrote the 1945 allegorical novella about farmyard animals overthrowing their human owner.

clue.text: Play parts musical's lead turned down

indicators.note: the leading letter is sent lower down the word, so the order of letters changes

parts.note: Cats is the Lloyd Webber musical based on T. S. Eliot's poems

explanation.surface: A musical's star has rejected the roles on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' reads as the star performer, but it is the first letter, which drops one place. 'Play parts' sounds like roles; it means the divisions of a drama.
explanation.definitionFit: A drama is divided into major sections, each of which is one of these, so they are parts of a play.

clue.text: Island priest must ring artist in Oz, perhaps

indicators.note: a ring encircles something, so the outer pieces surround the next one

parts.note: Is. is the map abbreviation for island
Eli is the priest who raised Samuel in the Old Testament
RA is a Royal Academician, a crossword artist

explanation.surface: A cleric on an island visits an artist living in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: Oz is not Australia here but the novelist Amos Oz. The island and priest join together and take the artist inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Amos Oz was a celebrated novelist from Jerusalem, so he is an example of a citizen of that country.

clue.text: "The sky above the port was the colour of television, tuned to —." (William Gibson, Neuromancer)

definitions.text: The sky above the port was the colour of television
definitions.meaning: surface reading: a quotation about a grey, flickering sky
setter's reading: complete the famous opening sentence of Gibson's cyberpunk novel

explanation.walkthrough: A general-knowledge fill-in: the missing words end the first sentence of Neuromancer (1984), comparing the sky to an untuned screen of grey static.
explanation.definitionFit: An old television set to a frequency with no broadcast shows only grey static, the image Gibson borrows.

clue.text: He put an end to Tom Jones taking questions

definitions.text: He put an end to Tom Jones
definitions.note: a surname for a person, as the clue's 'He'
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the novelist who wrote, and finished, The History of Tom Jones
second meaning: dealing with queries as they come, like catching balls

explanation.surface: Someone silenced the Welsh singer by opening the floor to questions.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Jones sounds like the singer, but it is the 1749 novel; putting an end to it means writing its last page.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry the novelist wrote the comic novel, and to field questions is to handle them, as a cricketer handles the ball.

clue.text: Foxville's king gets worked up with ruddy skin

indicators.note: worked up means agitated and stirred, so these letters are churned into a new order

parts.note: to get money is to earn it

indicators.note: the skin is only the outside, so just the outer letters are kept and the inside goes

parts.note: ruddy means red in colour

explanation.surface: The ruler of a town of foxes flushes red with agitation.
explanation.walkthrough: Ruddy gives a colour, and only its outer letters survive. The answer is the French name for the fox of medieval fable.
explanation.definitionFit: In the medieval beast epic, the trickster fox is the cunning lord of his kind, hence king of a fox town.

clue.text: "Who is John —?" (Ayn Rand, Atlas Shrugged)

definitions.meaning: surface reading: a question about some unidentified man called John
setter's reading: complete the catchphrase repeated throughout Rand's 1957 novel

explanation.walkthrough: A general-knowledge fill-in: the question is the opening line and running catchphrase of Atlas Shrugged, asked of its mysterious hero.
explanation.definitionFit: The inventor who leads the strike of creative minds in Rand's novel carries this surname, the subject of the refrain.

clue.text: Against eating at work? No, I could have lost weight!

indicators.note: what is eaten goes inside the eater, so one piece is taken into another

parts.note: anti means opposed to
a machine that is working is switched on
no means nothing, and nothing is zero, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A dieter who refuses to snack at the office boasts about the weight they might have lost.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation is spoken by the merchant of Venice, whose bond with Shylock put a pound of his flesh at stake.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's merchant pledged a pound of flesh as security for a loan, so he nearly lost weight literally.

clue.text: Poet who laments half-baked rotten dish

indicators.note: something half-baked is badly made and unfinished, so these letters are not in their proper form

parts.note: the two words taken as written

explanation.surface: A poet grieves over a meal that came out undercooked and spoiled.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a kitchen disaster; the dish is just letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A threnody is a song or poem of mourning, so its composer is a writer of verse lamenting the dead.

clue.text: This type of opera is of little worth

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the word in the title of Brecht and Weill's 1928 musical play
second meaning: cheap and trifling, like a coin worth three old pennies

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses a whole genre of opera as worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: A threepenny bit was a small pre-decimal British coin, hence the sense of cheapness.
explanation.definitionFit: Brecht's play with Weill's score carries the word in its title, and the coin's tiny value made it mean paltry.

clue.text: Step out of a place Louis's twin knew well?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to move, rouse oneself and set off

definitions.text: a place Louis's twin knew well
definitions.meaning: second meaning: slang for prison, where the Man in the Iron Mask was held

explanation.surface: A man walks out of somewhere the twin of a French king once knew.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dumas's tale, Louis XIV's twin Philippe is locked away in the Bastille wearing an iron mask.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang word for jail fits the masked twin's long imprisonment, and as a verb it means to bestir and move.

clue.text: "Vaughan died yesterday in his —." (J.G. Ballard)

definitions.meaning: surface reading: a report of a man's death in some unnamed setting
setter's reading: complete the opening sentence of Ballard's 1973 novel Crash

explanation.walkthrough: A general-knowledge fill-in: Crash opens with the death of Vaughan, the novel's obsessive, in the final one of his staged collisions.
explanation.definitionFit: Ballard's character fetishises motorway collisions, so his death comes in the final smash of many.

clue.text: Eyre's cruel aunt is always contrary, note

indicators.note: contrary means going the opposite way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, meaning always
D is a note of the musical scale

explanation.surface: Jane's unkind aunt is forever being awkward, it is noted.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'contrary' describe the aunt's temper, but it turns the poetic word for always around.
explanation.definitionFit: Mrs Reed is Jane's harsh guardian aunt at Gateshead Hall in Charlotte Brontë's novel.

clue.text: Silver relative planted on flash swordsman

parts.note: to dart is to move in a flash
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
a nan is a grandmother

explanation.surface: A flashy fencer has a silver-haired relative set beside him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Planted on' puts the first two pieces after the third in a down-style order: the flash comes first, silver and relative follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Dumas's Gascon hero joins the three musketeers and is renowned for his skill with a rapier.

clue.text: Worst Dr Who? That could the flowery-talking chap!

indicators.note: asking what something could become invites the letters to be rearranged into another form

parts.note: the three words taken as written

explanation.surface: Fans debate which actor was the worst Doctor Who and who talked the most nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flowery-talking' suggests florid speech, but it points to the poet of daffodils; the clue drops a 'be' after 'could'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Romantic poet wrote the famous lines on wandering lonely as a cloud among daffodils, so his verse literally talks of flowers.

clue.text: She put out Squire Arden in old Plath novel

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old

indicators.note: novel means new and different, so these letters take a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
the poet's surname taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman published a squire's story within an old Sylvia Plath novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a noun naming The Bell Jar, but it is an adjective signalling new order. 'Put out' means published.
explanation.definitionFit: Margaret Oliphant, the prolific Victorian Scottish writer, published Squire Arden in 1871.

clue.text: For court and duke, I told a handmaid's tale

parts.note: for as in a price: on sale for a pound is at a pound
to court a lover is to woo them
D is the abbreviation for duke

explanation.surface: A servant recounts gossip she spread about the royal court and its duke.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the author speaking in the first person about her best-known novel, The Handmaid's Tale.
explanation.definitionFit: Margaret the Canadian novelist wrote the 1985 dystopia The Handmaid's Tale, so she can claim to have told it.

clue.text: At sea, eager writer describes a beautiful boat's colour

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to draw round it, so one piece goes around another

parts.note: a pen is a writing tool

indicators.note: to be at sea is to be confused and lost, so these letters are muddled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A keen author out on the ocean writes about the colour of a lovely vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Lear's owl and pussycat went to sea in a beautiful boat of this colour; 'At sea' is the anagram signal, not a setting.
explanation.definitionFit: Lear's nonsense poem says the owl and the pussycat sailed in a beautiful boat painted that pale yellowish green.

clue.text: Quiet husband in thrall to European nymph

indicators.note: someone in thrall to another is held captive by them, so these pieces are held inside

parts.note: a Dane is a person from Denmark
p is piano, the musical direction for quiet
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A meek husband is enslaved by a European nymph.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes it a man under a nymph's spell; the quiet husband simply goes inside the Scandinavian.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the naiad fled Apollo and was turned into a laurel tree, a classic nymph story.

clue.text: Better travelling around with a valet, Jean?

definitions.meaning: surface reading: an improvement on going round the world, or a better way of touring
setter's reading: a man who made a wager, then circled the globe with his French manservant

explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' is not a comparison but one who bets. Verne's Fogg wagered he could go round the world in eighty days, taking his valet Jean Passepartout.
explanation.definitionFit: Verne's hero bet his club twenty thousand pounds on the journey and travelled with a servant, so he is a gambling traveller.

clue.text: Drink manly maiden chucked over Argos boss

indicators.note: something chucked over is flipped head over heels, so the letters face the other way

parts.note: to sup is to drink
male means masculine
M is a maiden over in cricket scoring

explanation.surface: A manly drinker has thrown a girl over for the boss of a catalogue shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Argos is a British catalogue retailer, which the surface plays on, but here it is the Greek city. A maiden is a cricket over with no runs.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the seer won a third of the kingdom of Argos as his reward, so he was one of its rulers.

clue.text: Expert player squandering a lead in The Crucible

parts.note: a pro is a professional, an expert

indicators.note: to squander is to throw away, so a letter is lost

parts.note: an actor plays a part
taken as written

explanation.surface: A skilled performer fluffs the leading role in Arthur Miller's play.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as an actor wasting a starring role; 'a lead' splits into the letter thrown away and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: John is the farmer at the centre of Miller's Salem witch-trial drama, its protagonist.

clue.text: Cathedral planner not against taking on English brickie?

indicators.note: to take on staff is to bring them in, so a letter is added inside
not denies what follows, so that piece is taken away

parts.note: Raymond Carver wrote the story collection Cathedral
v is versus, against
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A cathedral's designer, no opponent, hires an English bricklayer.
explanation.walkthrough: Cathedral suggests Wren, but it is a book by the American writer Raymond Carver. A brickie is a bricklayer, so the definition is a trade by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Bricklaying is a working life someone may follow, so the question mark marks the definition as an example of a profession.

clue.text: London-set novel: vampy parody of Zadie's debut?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a novel set down by Jack London, not one set in the city
second meaning: Zadie Smith's first novel White Teeth, given a vampire's dental twist

explanation.surface: Pitching a vampire spoof of a famous London novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'London-set' looks like a novel set in the capital, which White Teeth is, but it means one by Jack London about a wolf-dog in the Yukon.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack London's 1906 wolf-dog story has this title, and a vampire's pointed tooth replaces the teeth in Smith's debut.

clue.text: Argument going on about Ted Hughes's character

parts.note: c is circa, about
a row is a quarrel

explanation.surface: A dispute rumbles on about the nature of the poet Ted Hughes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests Hughes's personality, but it is a figure from his poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: Hughes's 1970 sequence follows a trickster bird figure through creation myths, the central persona of the book.

clue.text: His artwork aged badly, being dull so they said

indicators.note: reporting what people said points to spoken sound rather than spelling

parts.note: a dull sky or colour is grey

explanation.surface: An artist's work faded as it aged and was called dull.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilde's Dorian stays young while his portrait in the attic decays.
explanation.definitionFit: In Wilde's novel, Dorian's painted portrait ages and grows hideous in his place, so his artwork aged badly.

clue.text: Listen to forward royal, the woman's a titan

definitions.note: read as a description: she is a Titaness, a female Titan

indicators.note: royal stands for R, the royal abbreviation, and forward sends that last letter to the front

parts.note: to hear is to listen to

explanation.surface: An instruction to heed a pushy royal, since the lady is a giant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forward royal' moves the R at the end of HEAR, the R being the usual abbreviation for royal, up to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhea is one of the Titans of Greek myth, the mother of Zeus, so a female titan.

clue.text: Police often brace one of Magwitch's kind

indicators.note: to police something is to control and order it, so these letters are put into a new order

parts.note: the two words taken as written

explanation.surface: Officers often grab a convict like Magwitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Police' reads as a noun for officers, but it is a verb. Magwitch is the escaped convict in Great Expectations who secretly funds Pip.
explanation.definitionFit: Magwitch is Pip's anonymous patron, financing him as a gentleman, so he is a classic secret giver of money.

clue.text: Bad reaction to ham appearing at Christmas event?

definitions.meaning: surface reading: food poisoning or an allergy after eating festive gammon
setter's reading: the audience's noise for an over-acting villain at a pantomime

explanation.walkthrough: A ham is an over-the-top actor, not meat. Pantomime is a British Christmas stage show where audiences jeer the villain on cue.
explanation.definitionFit: Panto audiences greet the villain's entrance with a sibilant jeer, an expected show of disapproval.

clue.text: Honest and resilient clue-solving kid

parts.note: frank means candid and truthful
hardy means tough and able to endure

explanation.surface: Describes a truthful, tough child who is good at puzzles.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hardy Boys are teenage detectives in a long-running American series of mystery books.
explanation.definitionFit: The elder of the Hardy Boys brothers solves mysteries with his sibling Joe, a teenage sleuth following clues.
